children: MARKET WRAPS
STOCKS: Stocks fell as oil futures and Treasury yields continued to surge.
TREASURYS: Treasury yields rose, and the yield on the 10-year note closed at the highest level since July 2007.
FOREX: The U.S. dollar rose against rivals in anticipation of a Federal Reserve rate hike on Wednesday.
COMMODITIES: Oil futures rose by more than 4% to top $105 a barrel in New York, amid fears that Saudi export capacity will be constrained for an extended period.
HEADLINES
An AI bubble is no longer Wall Street's biggest fear. This stock-market
risk just took its place.
Global fund managers are being haunted by a new worry - the
possibility that bond yields could shoot higher in a "disorderly" manner,
stoking volatility that potentially spills over into stocks and the
economy.
That's according to Bank of America's September survey of 170 managers
who collectively have $470 billion in assets under management. Up from a
net 27% in August, 33% of those managers now see uncontrolled rises in
yields as the biggest "tail risk" facing them at present. A tail risk
refers to a rare or extreme market event that has a low probability of
happening.
Iran War's Price Tag, Pegged at $38 Billion, Is Growing as Much as $3
Billion a Month
WASHINGTON-The Pentagon spent some $38 billion in its first few months
of the war with Iran and will need at least five years to replace the
missile interceptors it expended trying to defend U.S. troops and bases,
according to a nonpartisan congressional office.
The Congressional Budget Office also estimates that the war is likely
to cost an additional $2 billion to $3 billion a month. The tally doesn't
include the costs of rebuilding U.S. bases damaged in the war and could
increase if fighting intensifies.
The assessment comes as President Trump is trying to determine next
steps in the war. Iran hasn't agreed to his demands to relinquish its
nuclear program, and Trump in recent weeks has tried to pivot to economic
pressure.
U.S. Diesel Prices Hit New Record High as Fuel Squeeze Bites
The average price of a gallon of diesel in the U.S. hit a fresh record
high of $6.27 on Tuesday, according to the American Automobile
Association.
U.S. diesel prices are soaring once again as the squeeze in the fuel
market tightens, breaching $6 a gallon for the first time on Friday.
Higher prices at the pump come as Brent Crude trades at around $107 a
barrel, with renewed supply concerns mounting and Northern Hemisphere
farmers entering the diesel-intensive harvesting season.
Prices had jumped at the start of the Iran conflict before cooling
after refiners ramped up production. The average price for a gallon of
diesel was $3.69 a year ago.
Regulators Press Tesla on Whether Cybercab May Have Option for Human
Control
Federal regulars are pressing Tesla on whether its steering wheel-free
Cybercab may have a way for humans to drive it after all.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration asked Tesla in an
order published Tuesday whether the vehicle has the ability to be driven
with traditional controls and, if so, whether that is why Tesla believes
the Cybercab is compliant with federal safety standards.
"State whether temporarily installed human driver controls or other
equipment for use by a human driver were a part of Tesla's basis for
certifying compliance," NHTSA said in the order.
Landmark Crypto Bill Fails Procedural Vote, Casting Doubt on New
Digital-Asset Rules
In a setback for the crypto industry, a bill that would have helped
usher digital assets into the mainstream financial system failed to
advance in Congress.
Known as the Clarity Act, the measure fell short Tuesday in a
procedural vote requiring the approval of 60 senators.
The legislation, which was expected to establish the first
comprehensive regulatory framework for digital assets, was under
negotiation for more than a year. Democrats and Republicans fought over
whether the measure should restrict President Trump from profiting off
the industry. Crypto and banking executives (and their allies) meanwhile
dug in on whether digital-asset platforms such as Coinbase could offer
tokens with interest-like rewards that resembled bank deposits.
Truist to Sell $5.5 Billion of Loans as It Exits Near-Prime Auto Lending
Truist Financial has inked a deal to sell $5.5 billion of auto loans
as part of the regional bank's decision to exit the near-prime auto
lending business.
Truist on Tuesday said it expects the sale, which represents
substantially all assets of its Regional Acceptance auto-finance unit, to
generate net proceeds of $5.2 billion, along with a $535 million
loan-loss-reserve recapture.
Regional Acceptance generated breakeven pretax earnings in the first
half of the year, Truist said.
Fed System Monitoring Banks Suffered Outage Last Month
A Federal Reserve database used for monitoring banks experienced a
temporary outage last month, triggering concerns from a top Senate
Democrat about the consequences of cuts to the Fed's regulatory staff.
The Fed confirmed that part of the system, called the National
Information Center, had an outage last month.
"The August 5 outage temporarily impacted the National Information
Center's public website," a Fed spokesperson said. "Critical functions
remained operational."
TALKING POINT Bond Yields Could Come Down as Fast as They've Climbed

Sometimes, the simplest explanation for something works. And in the case of the Treasury market, it appears that the main reason bond yields are rising is because short-term interest rates are likely to rise.

There are many risks that can frighten the bond market. Runaway inflation. Unsustainable fiscal deficits. Excessive bond issuance by tech companies. And as 10-year Treasury yields have climbed toward 5%, there has been no shortage of headlines about those threats.

But another reason investors sell longer-term bonds and demand a higher yield to hold them is because they believe that rates on shorter-term bonds are going to be paying them more for a while. So to agree to lock up their money for longer, they need more payback.
Based on available market signals, this appears to be the main factor behind the move in recent weeks. And that in turn is determined by what the Federal Reserve is expected to do.
That may be little comfort to anyone hoping to get a mortgage or borrow money. Yet it does suggest that at least some of the recent move is reversible, too.

Measures of inflation expectations, for example, haven't jumped dramatically very recently. The gap between the yield on a nominal 10-year Treasury bond and the yield over inflation paid on 10-year Treasury Inflation Protected Securities is around 2.4%. This so-called "break even" inflation rate is higher than it was in 2019 or early 2020, when it was under 2%. But it is well within the range of where it has traded since 2021.

This yield gap isn't a perfect measure of expectations for inflation, since it can also reflect differences in liquidity between the two markets and other factors. However, it matches what other measures of expectations show.
Telis Demos, The Wall Street Journal
